nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the mythic lyric and the autobiography of lost Eden
literary_identity: Poet, critic and translator; the great Orcadian lyric poet of the century and the author of The Story and the Fable, one of the finest Scottish autobiographies.
biography: Born Edwin Muir on a farm at Deerness, Orkney, on 15 May 1887; the family moved to Glasgow in 1901 and was destroyed by the city's poverty, an experience that became the ground of all his poetry. He worked as a clerk in a bone factory and an office, married Willa Anderson in 1919, translated Kafka with her, wrote criticism for The Freeman, the New Age and The Listener, and published First Poems (1925), The Narrow Place (1943), The Voyage (1946) and One Foot in Eden (1956). He died at Swaffham Prior, Cambridgeshire, on 3 January 1959.
literary_profile: Muir is the great Scottish poet of the modern lyric: his poems of Eden, the fall, the journey and the lost childhood are among the finest in twentieth-century English, and The Story and the Fable (1940) is one of the great autobiographies of the period. With his wife Willa he translated Kafka's novels into English for the first time, an act of transmission as important as his own verse.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, mythic, unnervingly simple lyric; the dream image held in regular stanza; the archetype deployed without ornament; the child's vision and the adult's guilt; the prose of an autobiography that reads like a fable.
intellectual_concerns: Eden, the fall and the lost childhood; the city and the destruction of the family; the journey, the voyage and the dream; Scotland, Orkney and the inheritance of myth; time, dream and the archetypal image; the poet's vocation.
historical_significance: Muir is the finest Scottish lyric poet of the period and one of the great autobiographers: his mythic poems of Eden and the journey are permanent, The Story and the Fable is a central Scottish autobiography, and his translations of Kafka gave English the writer who remade the modern novel.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the experimental prose, the portrait and the syntax of repetition
literary_identity: Writer and patron; the great American experimentalist of the period, the host of the Paris salon that made the Lost Generation, and the inventor of a prose without nouns.
biography: Born Gertrude Stein in Allegheny, Pennsylvania, on 3 February 1874 into a wealthy German-Jewish family; she studied at Radcliffe under William James and at Johns Hopkins medicine, moved to Paris in 1903 with her brother Leo, and began collecting the paintings that made 27 rue de Fleurus the centre of modern art. Three Lives appeared in 1909, Tender Buttons in 1914, The Making of Americans in 1925 and The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas in 1933. She lived with Alice B. Toklas from 1907 and died at Neuilly-sur-Seine on 27 July 1946.
literary_profile: Stein is the great experimentalist of the period: her 'continuous present', her repetition, her abolition of the noun and her cubist portraits made a prose that dismantles the conventions of English syntax, and she taught a generation of American writers — Hemingway among them — how to write a sentence. The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas is one of the period's most entertaining books, and her Paris salon was the social centre of modernism.
stylistic_characteristics: The continuous present and the deliberate repetition; the abolition of the noun and the article; the portrait made of repeated traits; the cubist arrangement of phrases; the plain declarative sentence used against its own grammar; the memoir written as a joke and a history at once.
intellectual_concerns: The making of Americans and the American family; the ordinary object and the ordinary life; the Paris of the avant-garde; genius, patronage and the woman artist; the war and the occupation; language itself as a subject.
historical_significance: Stein is the central American experimental writer of the period: Three Lives and Tender Buttons changed the possibilities of English prose, her Paris salon made modernism a social fact, The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas is a permanent memoir, and her influence on Hemingway, Anderson and the American sentence is beyond calculation.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the small-town story and the American grotesque
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of Winesburg, Ohio, the book that gave American fiction its modern small-town story and its term for the inarticulate outsider.
biography: Born Sherwood Anderson in Camden, Ohio, on 13 September 1876; he left school at fourteen, served in the Spanish-American War, ran a paint factory in Elyria, Ohio, and in 1912 walked out of it in a nervous collapse to become a writer. Windy McPherson's Son (1916) and Marching Men (1917) preceded Winesburg, Ohio (1919), which made his name; he published many novels and stories, edited two little magazines, and died in Panama on 8 March 1941.
literary_profile: Anderson wrote the book that made the modern American short story possible: Winesburg, Ohio gave American fiction the small town as a place of hidden loneliness — the 'grotesques' whose truth is not told — and its influence runs through Hemingway, Faulkner, Wolfe and Carver. He was the first American writer to make the inarticulate the subject of the form.
stylistic_characteristics: The plain, bare, repetitive sentence; the story without plot, built on a single moment of longing; the recurring town and the recurring characters; the framed sequence of stories as a novel; the voice of a man who cannot say what he means.
intellectual_concerns: The small town and its hidden lives; loneliness and the failure of speech; sex, adolescence and the fear of the body; the industrial town against the old agrarian America; the artist and the escape from the town; the grotesque and the truth of the outsider.
historical_significance: Anderson wrote the founding book of the modern American short story: Winesburg, Ohio changed what an American story could be about, gave American fiction the small town as a place of hidden lives, and was acknowledged by Hemingway, Faulkner and Wolfe as the source of their generation's prose.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the blues poem, the Harlem Renaissance lyric and the satire of the colour line
literary_identity: Poet, novelist, playwright and columnist; the central poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the first American to make the blues a literary form, and the most widely read Black writer of the century.
biography: Born James Mercer Langston Hughes in Joplin, Missouri, on 1 February 1902; he was raised by his grandmother in Lawrence, Kansas, and his mother in Illinois and Ohio, spent a year at Columbia, worked as a ship's cook and a busboy, and was 'discovered' in a Washington restaurant by Vachel Lindsay in 1925. The Weary Blues appeared in 1926 and Fine Clothes to the Jew in 1927; he wrote the novel Not Without Laughter (1930), the play Mulatto (1935), the Jesse B. Semple stories and the Montage of a Dream Deferred (1951). He died in New York on 22 May 1967.
literary_profile: Hughes is the central poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the first American poet to make the blues and jazz a literary form: The Weary Blues put the blues on the printed page, 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers', 'I, Too' and 'Harlem' are among the most quoted American poems, and his Jesse B. Semple columns made a Black vernacular voice a national institution. He wrote for the whole race, not for the salon, and that is the source of his permanence.
stylistic_characteristics: The blues stanza and the jazz line; the plain vernacular speech of Harlem; the repetition-with-variation of the blues form; the short ironic lyric with a withheld pain; the comic monologue (Simple); the poem that asks a question instead of making a statement.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line and the New Negro; Harlem and the Great Migration; the blues, jazz and the pleasure economy; the dream deferred and the American promise; the working Black man and the comic survivor (Semple); Africa, the South and the ancestral past.
historical_significance: Hughes is the central African American poet of the century and the founding figure of the Harlem Renaissance in verse: he made the blues a literary form, wrote the period's most quoted poems of Black America, created the Jesse B. Semple voice, and maintained a public Black poetry for four decades when almost no one else did.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the folk novel, the anthropology of the Black South and the woman's voice
literary_identity: Novelist, folklorist and anthropologist; the great recorder of Black Southern folk culture and the author of Their Eyes Were Watching God, the finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance.
biography: Born in Notasulga, Alabama, on 7 January 1891 and raised in Eatonville, Florida, the first incorporated Black town in America; she worked as a maid, a waitress and a manicurist, studied at Howard and at Barnard under Franz Boas, and did fieldwork in Florida, New Orleans and Haiti. Jonah's Gourd Vine (1934), Mules and Men (1935), Their Eyes Were Watching God (1937), Tell My Horse (1938) and Moses, Man of the Mountain (1939) followed; she died in poverty at Fort Pierce, Florida, on 28 January 1960, and her work was recovered by Alice Walker in the 1970s.
literary_profile: Hurston wrote the finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance and the great record of Black Southern folk culture: Their Eyes Were Watching God made a Black woman's voice and a Black woman's desire the centre of an American novel, and Mules and Men preserved a body of folklore that would otherwise have been lost. Her prose — the free indirect rendering of Eatonville speech — is one of the period's great achievements.
stylistic_characteristics: Free indirect style that renders Black Southern speech without condescension; the frame of the tale-teller and the 'lying' session; the folk idiom transcribed as literature; the metaphor drawn from the natural world; the novel structured by a woman's marriages.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the Black South and the folk community; the Black woman's desire and self-making; marriage, work and independence; the Eatonville town and its 'lying' culture; the hurricane, nature and God; the migration north and the return south.
historical_significance: Hurston wrote the finest African American novel of the period and the greatest record of Black Southern folklore: Their Eyes Were Watching God is a permanent American novel, Mules and Men preserved a whole oral culture, and her recovery in the 1970s made her the central woman writer of the Harlem Renaissance.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Jamaican-American; the protest sonnet, the Jamaican dialect poem and the novel of Black labour
literary_identity: Poet and novelist; the first major poet of the Harlem Renaissance, the author of 'If We Must Die' and Home to Harlem.
biography: Born Festus Claudius McKay in Clarendon Parish, Jamaica, on 15 September 1889; he was apprenticed to a wheelwright and then served in the Jamaican constabulary, published Songs of Jamaica and Constab Ballads in 1912, and came to the United States to study at Tuskegee and Kansas State. He moved to Harlem in 1914, published 'If We Must Die' in 1919, Harlem Shadows in 1922, and the novels Home to Harlem (1928), Banjo (1929) and Banana Bottom (1933); he travelled to Russia and France, became a Catholic, and died in Chicago on 22 May 1948.
literary_profile: McKay is the first major poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the author of the period's most famous protest poem: 'If We Must Die' — written during the Red Summer of 1919 and quoted by Churchill in 1940 — gave the movement its trumpet call, Harlem Shadows its first substantial book of verse, and Home to Harlem the first best-selling Black novel of the decade. His Jamaican dialect poems are the first body of West Indian verse in English.
stylistic_characteristics: The sonnet and the ballad used for protest; the Jamaican dialect written phonetically; the blunt, direct, unornamented statement; the image of the body under threat; the travel narrative of the Black migrant worker.
intellectual_concerns: Race and the colour line; the Black worker and the colonial inheritance; the Jamaican folk and the peasantry; Harlem, the cabaret and the migrant's city; the body, desire and the police; the revolutionary and the exile.
historical_significance: McKay wrote the period's most famous protest poem and the first substantial body of verse of the Harlem Renaissance: 'If We Must Die' became an international anthem of resistance, Harlem Shadows gave the movement its first book, and his Jamaican dialect poems founded West Indian literature in English.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the lyric in the English tradition and the poetry of the colour line
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and anthologist; the most formally accomplished poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the movement's principal defender of the inherited English lyric.
biography: Born Countee LeRoy Porter in New York on 30 May 1903 and raised in Harlem by the Reverend Frederick Asbury Cullen; he won prizes at high school and at New York University, published Color in 1925, graduated from Harvard in 1926, and edited Caroling Dusk (1927), the anthology of Black verse. He married Yolande Du Bois in 1928, taught in the New York schools, and published Copper Sun (1927), The Black Christ (1929), One Way to Heaven (1932) and The Medea and Some Poems (1935). He died in New York on 9 January 1946.
literary_profile: Cullen is the most formally gifted poet of the Harlem Renaissance: Color and Copper Sun contain the finest English lyrics written by an African American of the period, and 'Yet Do I Marvel', 'Heritage' and 'Incident' are permanent poems of the colour line. His editorship of Caroling Dusk gave the movement its anthology, and his insistence that a Black poet might use the whole English tradition was the counter-position to Hughes's folk programme.
stylistic_characteristics: The strict English lyric — the sonnet, the ballad, the quatrain and the rhymed octave; the Keatsian and Housmanesque diction; the irony of a formal grace turned on a brutal subject; the refrain and the clanging rhyme; the poem that ends on a question.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line and the burden of a 'double consciousness'; Africa and the ancestral inheritance; the lynch mob and the murdered child; the Christian faith and the Black church; love and the private life; the poet's quarrel with his own tradition.
historical_significance: Cullen is the most formally accomplished poet of the Harlem Renaissance and the author of some of its finest lyrics: Color and Copper Sun are permanent books of American verse, 'Yet Do I Marvel' and 'Heritage' are central poems of the colour line, and Caroling Dusk is the movement's defining anthology.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the modernist collage of the Black South and the lyric of passing
literary_identity: Poet and novelist; the author of Cane, the most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American modernist texts.
biography: Born Nathan Pinchback Toomer in Washington, D.C., on 26 December 1894, the grandson of a Reconstruction governor of Louisiana and the great-grandson of a slave; he studied at the University of Wisconsin, the Massachusetts College of Agriculture, the American Physical Training College, the University of Chicago and the City College of New York without taking a degree, and taught for a term at a Black school in Sparta, Georgia, in 1921. Cane appeared in 1923; he later joined the Gurdjieff movement, wrote largely unpublished work, became a Quaker, and died at Doylestown, Pennsylvania, on 30 January 1967.
literary_profile: Toomer wrote the most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance: Cane — a collage of stories, poems and a play, moving from the Black South to the urban North — is one of the great modernist texts in American literature, and its lyric prose anticipates both Faulkner and Hurston. It is the only major book of the movement that refuses the novel's form altogether.
stylistic_characteristics: The collage of genres (story, poem, drama) in a single book; the lyric prose-poem with a refrain; the crescent-shaped page and the modernist typography; the abrupt shift from the Southern field to the Northern street; the image that returns across the book.
intellectual_concerns: The Black South and the Georgia cane field; the migration north and the urban crowd; race, passing and mixed descent; the woman as a figure of the land; the loss of the folk world; the artist's separation from his own people.
historical_significance: Toomer wrote the most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American modernist texts: Cane invented a collage form that American fiction is still absorbing, its lyric prose changed the sound of Black American writing, and it is the only major book of the movement that is formally as advanced as Ulysses or The Waste Land.
